standfirst: An ex-convict opens a bar in Itaewon to bury the conglomerate that killed his father, and for three episodes it is as good as K-drama underdog writing gets. After that it comes apart. The female lead is written into a corner, the love triangle eats the plot, and the time skip hands away every bit of momentum the first three episodes built. These six take the parts that actually worked and do them without the second half.

picks.why: The revenge Itaewon Class kept promising and then mislaid. A man given another run at a chaebol family from the inside, with the plotting kept front and centre for the full sixteen and antagonists drawn with real detail instead of one snarling chairman. Song Joong-ki plays the outsider who is smarter than the room, which is what Saeroyi was sold as. Difference: the register is corporate satire, and the final episode makes a choice that retroactively cheapens the sixteen hours in front of it.

For the found family of misfits above a business, which is the thing people miss about Danbam. A building full of tenants nobody else would defend, an outsider who arrives with money and no patience, and a conglomerate that has to be dismantled floor by floor. Difference: it is a black comedy that enjoys itself, so the dignity and the grief that made Saeroyi's story land are simply not on the menu.

If what you actually responded to was a man with nothing being taken seriously at work. A contract employee with no degree inside a trading company with no room for him, and the same conviction that small competences are worth a whole scene. If Saeroyi lucking into his wins bothered you, nothing here is luck. Difference: no revenge, no romance, not even ambiguous romance, and the tone is stoic where Itaewon Class is loud.

The righteous-outsider-versus-corrupt-money plot with the tone deliberately cranked to farce. A short-tempered priest, a useless detective, a neighbourhood worth protecting, and a genuinely satisfying dismantling of people who assumed they were untouchable. Difference: it is a comedy first and it never asks to be taken as seriously as Itaewon Class asks to be taken.

The same anger at predatory money, stripped to eight episodes and two friends. Boxers against a loan shark, a mentor worth avenging, and no time at all for a love triangle. Difference: it is a fight show. There is no business to build and no slow climb, just consequences arriving quickly.

For anyone who finished Itaewon Class annoyed that the revenge kept getting deferred. Victims the system failed, an episodic revenge service, a very satisfying beating roughly every second week. Difference: no long game and no cost. Where Saeroyi needed fifteen years, this needs two episodes, and it is pulp on purpose.

against.title: Crash Landing on You
against.why: The most common accidental pairing, because both were the big Netflix Korean hit of early 2020 and one autoplays into the other. It is a bad swap. One is a high-concept romance engineered to be safe; the other is a grudge story with a bleak first act.

against.title: Start-Up
against.why: Suggested because both are about building a business from nothing with a young ensemble. Start-Up is a romance with a pitch deck: the company exists to give the love triangle somewhere to happen. Itaewon Class means the business. If you came for the ledger and the rent, this will frustrate you.

against.title: Reply 1988
against.why: Paired for the ragtag-chosen-family warmth of the Danbam staff. But Reply 1988 has no antagonist and nothing to win, and its whole method is safety. Itaewon Class is a revenge plot where the found family keeps getting sacrificed to it. Same shelf, opposite function.
